newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine says fugitive ex-PM can return from Israel.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine says fugitive ex-PM can return from Israel.

text.p: Ukrainian lawmakers restored parliamentary immunity on Wednesday to a fugitive former prime minister accused of embezzling $25 million of public funds, clearing the way for his return from hiding in Israel.
Deputies voted 253 to 19 to grant immunity to Yefim Zvyagilsky, who was acting prime minister under Ukraine's first post-Soviet president, Leonid Kravchuk.

"This decision gives a chance for Zvyagilsky to return to Ukraine and to co-operate with the General Prosecutor's Office... (to decide) whether to close the case or to press ahead with it," said Petro Sheiko, who headed a special investigation group and met Zvyagilsky in Israel.

Under Wednesday's decision Zvyagilsky, who was elected deputy in 1994 in his coal-mining hometown of Donetsk in eastern Ukraine, must return to Kiev within two months or his immunity will be withdrawn.

Zvyagilsky, 64, is accused of siphoning off state funds through the illegal sale of 200,000 tonnes of aviation fuel and foreign exchange operations involving a bank his wife set up in the former Soviet republic.
Zvyagilsky, a former director of Ukraine's biggest coal pit, rejects the allegations and says he is prepared to return home in exchange for security guarantees and no "political retaliation."
"I felt that all possible and impossible sins in Ukraine were attributed to me," Zvyagilsky told the daily Kievskiye Vedomosti in Israel in an interview published on Wednesday.
"But the government was not a private shop but rather a strucure with collective responsibility, subordinate to the president and to parliament."
Ukrainian officials say Zvyagilsky, a Jew by origin, acquired an Israeli passport during his 2-1/2 years in Israel, but he denies this.
The Zvyagilsky issue has cast a shadow over otherwise cordial Ukrainian-Israeli relations, especially after Israel turned down Kiev's request to extradite Zvyagilsky two years ago.
Some top government officials, including Foreign Minister Hennady Udovenko, have suggested that Ukrainian authorities might have to think twice before appointing Jews to senior jobs in the future.
